raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the survival benefit of defibrillator therapy while avoiding transvenous leads, venous access, endovascular infection, lead extraction, and chronic lead failure. The system consists of a lateral thoracic pulse generator and a parasternal subcutaneous electrode; sensing is entirely extracardiac, and therapy is delivered as high-energy biphasic shocks with brief post-shock pacing. Early feasibility work showed reliable detection and conversion of induced ventricular fibrillation, establishing the concept of an entirely extrathoracic defibrillator [1]. Subsequent single-centre and multicentre experiences refined implant technique, screening, and programming while identifying early limitations, particularly T-wave oversensing, myopotential noise, discomfort, and lead migration [2], [3], [4].

Pivotal prospective data supported regulatory adoption. In the IDE study, the S-ICD met prespecified safety and efficacy endpoints, with high acute conversion efficacy and successful treatment of spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias [5]. The two-incision technique simplified implantation and eliminated the superior parasternal incision without compromising lead position [6]. Large registries then extended evidence beyond early adopters. EFFORTLESS demonstrated acceptable 30-day and 1-year complication-free rates, high shock efficacy, and a low frequency of later conversion to a pacing-capable system [7], [8], [9]. Five-year EFFORTLESS follow-up confirmed durable performance: final shock efficacy remained high, structural lead failure was rare, and only a small minority required replacement with a transvenous device for pacing indications [10].

Patient selection remains central. The S-ICD is best suited to patients with a standard ICD indication who do not need bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization therapy, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP). It is especially attractive for younger patients, those with limited venous access, prior device infection, congenital heart disease anatomy, inherited arrhythmia syndromes, or high lifetime risk of lead-related complications. Conversely, patients with recurrent monomorphic ventricular tachycardia likely to respond to ATP, symptomatic bradycardia, advanced conduction disease, or present or anticipated need for cardiac resynchronization are better served by transvenous, extravascular, or combined systems. UNTOUCHED helped address whether the S-ICD could be used in a more conventional primary-prevention low-ejection-fraction population; with standardized high-rate programming and contemporary sensing filters, inappropriate shock rates were lower than in early studies, while appropriate shock efficacy remained high [11].

The most definitive comparison with transvenous ICDs came from PRAETORIAN, designed as a randomized noninferiority trial in patients without pacing indications [12]. In 849 patients, the S-ICD was noninferior to the transvenous ICD for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [13]. Secondary analyses clarified the trade-off: absence of ATP increased the probability that a treated ventricular tachyarrhythmia would receive a shock, but total appropriate shocks and shock efficacy were similar, and ATP accelerated some ventricular tachycardias [14]. Device-related complications differed qualitatively; transvenous systems had more lead-related and systemic infectious complications, whereas S-ICD complications were more often pocket-related or related to sensing and device position [15]. Thus, the S-ICD is not a universally “safer ICD,” but a device with a distinct risk profile that is often preferable when pacing is unnecessary.

Post-approval studies have provided important real-world reassurance. The US S-ICD Post Approval Study confirmed long-term safety and efficacy across many centres, including operators with variable implant experience [16]. Early clinical-characteristics and perioperative analyses showed high implantation success and acceptable short-term adverse-event rates [17], and 1-year follow-up demonstrated continued efficacy with a contemporary patient mix [18]. Infection analyses suggested that S-ICD infections are usually localized and rarely associated with bacteraemia, supporting use in patients at high systemic infection risk [19]. Dialysis patients, a group with high vascular-access and infectious risk, had acceptable S-ICD performance, although their overall mortality and competing risks remain substantial [20].

Comparative observational analyses and quality-of-life studies broaden interpretation. Propensity-matched SIMPLE and EFFORTLESS analyses suggested broadly similar shock and complication outcomes between S-ICD and transvenous ICD recipients after adjustment [21]. Quality-of-life data did not show a major disadvantage of the S-ICD compared with transvenous systems, although pocket discomfort, body image, and shock anxiety remain important counselling topics [22]. Long-term Dutch experience emphasized generator longevity, replacement considerations, and the importance of meticulous follow-up [23]. Reviews and editorials have appropriately cautioned that avoidance of intravascular leads must be weighed against larger generators, lack of chronic pacing, longer time to therapy, and dependence on surface-electrogram screening and discrimination algorithms [24], [25], [26], [27].

Current guideline frameworks support S-ICD use in patients meeting ICD indications when pacing for bradycardia, resynchronization, or ATP is not required, particularly when venous access or infection risk is a concern [28], [29], [30]. Future directions include improved discrimination algorithms, smaller generators, longer battery life, better defibrillation testing strategies, integration with leadless pacing for ATP or bradycardia support, and competition from extravascular ICD systems. For now, the S-ICD is a mature, evidence-based alternative to transvenous ICD therapy: its value lies in careful selection, technically sound implantation, thoughtful programming, and shared decision-making that explicitly addresses the trade-off between avoiding transvenous leads and foregoing chronic pacing therapies.
